description:
포스테키안 핵심역량: 자기관리역량(100%)

미래 사회는 지식이나 정보가 증가하는 속도나 양이 급격하게 변화할 것으로 전망하고 있으며 더불어 인간 수명은 점차 길어질 것으로 예상되어 앞으로의 시대에 잘 적응하고 살아가기 위해서는 스스로 자신을 관리하는 능력을 가지고 있어야 한다.
본 강의의 목표는 수강생 전원을 대상으로 우수한 조법과 팀워크 외에도 체력과 지구력이 요구되는 종목입니다. 따라서 조정 수업을 통해 팔, 다리, 윗몸을 지속적으로 움직여야하는 전신운동으로 강인한 체력과 지구력 및 순발력이 향상되며, 일치된 호흡과 동작의 조화를 필요로 하여 학생들의 협동심과 단결력을 키우는데 도움이 된다. 이를 통해 신체적 측면에서는 자신의 체력을 스스로 관리하는 역량을 기르고 정신적인 측면에서는 사회성 발달을 통해 앞으로의 개인적, 사회적인 생활을 나가는데 중요한 의미가 된다.
prerequisites: 없음
Lesson Objectives:
포스테키안 핵심역량: 자기관리역량(100%)

미래 사회는 지식이나 정보가 증가하는 속도나 양이 급격하게 변화할 것으로 전망하고 있으며 더불어 인간 수명은 점차 길어질 것으로 예상되어 앞으로의 시대에 잘 적응하고 살아가기 위해서는 스스로 자신을 관리하는 능력을 가지고 있어야 한다.
본 강의의 목표는 수강생 전원을 대상으로 우수한 조법과 팀워크 외에도 체력과 지구력이 요구되는 종목입니다. 따라서 조정 수업을 통해 팔, 다리, 윗몸을 지속적으로 움직여야하는 전신운동으로 강인한 체력과 지구력 및 순발력이 향상되며, 일치된 호흡과 동작의 조화를 필요로 하여 학생들의 협동심과 단결력을 키우는데 도움이 된다. 이를 통해 신체적 측면에서는 자신의 체력을 스스로 관리하는 역량을 기르고 정신적인 측면에서는 사회성 발달을 통해 앞으로의 개인적, 사회적인 생활을 나가는데 중요한 의미가 된다.
Lecture progress plan:
1주
1. Orientation(교과목 및 개요 강의, 연구과제 부여)
2. 교과목 소개 및 개요 강의

2주 
1. 강의 목표: 조정종목의 유래 및 육상에서의 기본기 rowing ergometer 이용법
2. 강의 내용
- 기본동작 훈련: arms, arms body, seat2/1, stroke

3주
1. 강의 목표: Stroke 의 순서 이해 습득
2. 강의 내용
- 기본동작 훈련: finish, hands away, recovery, 
- 구분동작으로 자연스러운 동작 훈련

4주
1. 강의 목표: 로윙 stroke의 자연스러움 순서동작 향상 및 연결동작 자연구현
2. 강의 내용
- 구분동작으로 순서에 맞게 훈련, 앞뒤 움직임 진행순서 맞게 훈련

5주
1. 강의 목표: 수상안전교육 및 수상 기본테크닉 드라이브 연결
2. 강의 내용
- 보트를 들고 내리는 방법 숙지 및 배거치 타는 훈련
- 육상에서의 기본기 동작들을 보트를 계류한 상태에서 구분동작으로 진행훈련(arms, armsbody, seat2/1, stroke)

6주
1. 강의 목표: 수상에서의 자연스러운 연결 및 용어 숙지
2. 강의 내용
- 긴급시 취해야하는 행동들 숙지 
- 반복연습 구분동작 없이 자연스러운 드라이브 훈련

7주 
1. 강의 목표: 수상 실습 추진력 가속화 row 진행시 방향전환 이해
2. 강의 내용
- 수상에서의 1인 기본기 동작들 진행 훈련
- side 구별법 side stroke 전환 훈련

8주
- 중간고사

9주
1. 강의 목표: 페어별로 stroke 팀워크 및 단합력 이해
2. 강의 내용
- 페어별 stroke 진행, catch, middle, finish 중점 보완 및 브래드 깊이 훈련

10주 
1. 강의 목표: 공기저항 파도저항을 막기 위한 turn으로 인한 가속력 향상 
2. 강의 내용
- stroke 진행시 turn 포인트, 진행 후 올 높이처리
- 높은 파도에 무릎 지나 turn 훈련 

11주
1. 강의 목표: 4명의 cerw의 진행으로 팀워크 단합력 향상
2. 강의 내용
- all man rowing 및 밸런스 

12주
1. 강의 목표: all man rowing으로 진행시 자연스러운 물속 진행 향상
2. 강의 내용
- all man crew stroke 훈련, 구분동작 포함 turn 진행
- 4명의 노 높이 훈련, 무릎지나 turn catch 훈련

13주
1. 강의 목표: 가속도이해 향상 및 배 팀워크 단합력 발달
2. 강의 내용
- 강한 힘 전달 훈련, 스트로크 진행 가속도, 물밖 시트진행 훈련

14주
1. 강의 목표: 조정경기의 이해 및 체험
2. 강의 내용
- start진행 훈련, start 이후에 진행되는 stroke rate 훈련
- race 리허설

15주
- 실기시험: 배 승선법, stroke 진행(catch finish), 보트별 팀워크 단합력 가속도 평가

16주
- 기말고사
grading:
● 4회 이상 결석시 "F" (결석 1회당 2점 감점/지각 3회당 결석 1회로 인정)
1) 출석: 40%
2) 실기시험: 60%

3) POSTECH 체육교과목 홈페이지(http:// phyedu.postech.ac.kr)

description:
Postechian Core Capability: Global Citizen 100%

Purpose:  The purpose of this course is to improve the students’ ability to communicate in English professionally in various modes.

The course is designed to meet the expanding English needs of graduate students as global citizens and scholars/academics by exposing them to diverse language situations they will encounter in real life. Register, structures, and patterns will be introduced and modeled to effectively communicate in international lab & work situations from daily conversations, email writing, resumes and job interviews, phone calls and on and offline meetings to responding to issues, negotiating plans and projects, and articulating and presenting ideas. Students will be expected to work both individually and in groups to exchange ideas, to evaluate their peers, to lead group and class discussions, role plan and to summarize concepts and discussions, all of which will build students’ English confidence and competence to communicate naturally and effectively.
prerequisites: Any students with more than 5 absences will not be able to pass the class. If you are not able to attend class, or will be late, you must email me in advance AND  submit documentation as proof for the absence/ lateness to be excused. Otherwise, 2% will be deducted for each unexcused absence. Repeated lateness can affect your grade as an unexcused absence. Participation is checked through a combination of preparedness, attendance, in-class interactions, and peer-reviews. Missing an in-class assignment or peer-review session due to lateness or absence will result in the loss of those participation points.

description:
What is politics? Why do we need to understand it? If you think you know the answers to these questions but find yourself struggling to articulate them, then you do not truly understand politics. At first glance, politics may seem disconnected from our lives—a mere turf war among politicians that causes stress rather than providing any real benefit. You might wonder if there is any real need to understand something so unpleasant and headache-inducing. However, politics has a much greater impact on our lives than we realize, and furthermore, we are deeply involved in it, whether we know it or not. To be ignorant of politics, which is so intimately connected to our lives, is akin to leaving a crucial variable in our equation for achieving our goals as an unknown. The equations faced by diverse individuals are all unique. Therefore, this course cannot provide a universal solution that solves everyone's equation. Instead, it offers various useful tools to assist you in the process of finding the answers to solve your own unique equation. Based on the knowledge gained in this class, students are expected to independently solve the political equations they face in achieving their goals.

Postechian Core Competencies: Knowledge Exploration Competency, Creative Convergence Competency

grading:
Attendance (0%): There is no attendance score. However, 7 or more total absences will result in an automatic F grade.
Discussion Participation (10%): Participation in class discussions.
Midterm Exam (40%): Open-book, take-home format.
Final Exam (40%): Open-book, take-home format.
Final Book Review Assignment (10%): Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt, How Democracies Die, Across, 2018. 
Optional Mission: An A+ grade will be granted if you successfully publish a reader's contribution (op-ed) related to the topics covered in class in a major daily print newspaper (e.g., Chosun, JoongAng, Dong-A, Hankyoreh, Kyunghyang) before the final exam. description: 본 과목은 경제학에서 다루어지는 기본적인 개념을 세부적으로 검토하고 경제학의 기본원리와 시장 자본주의가 갖고 있는 과학성에 대한 문제와 사회적인 연관성을 살펴보게 될 것이다. 본 과목은 경제활동에 대한 정치학적이고 사회학적, 문화학적 그리고 인류학적인 접근이다. 경제학에서 현재 당연시 여기고 있는 개념과 현상 및 실제적인 사례에 대해서 사회/정치/문화/인류학적인 탐구를 통해서 어떻게 경제학적 개념이 형성되었으며, 어떻게 수행되고 있는가에 대해서 고찰하게 될 것이다. 특히, 경제학에서 다루고 있는 개념과 이론이 갖고 있는 고정적인 것으로 전제하고 심층적인 사회과학적 분석에서 제외되어온 문제를 역사화, 상대화 및 맥락화를 통해 문제를 해결할 것이다.

제 7주: 과학화된 경제학/재정학 – 규칙과 모델로 설명되는 자본주의의 형성과정

- Donald MacKenzie, 2006. An engine, not a camera – How financial models shape markets, MIT Press

제 8주: 사회적 구성물로서 시장/경제 – 사회적 합의와 행위자들의 필요에 의해 형성되는 시장/경제에 대한 사회학적 고찰

제 9주: 행위자 연결망 이론에서 본 시장/경제 – 과학기술학의 행위자 연결망이론의 경제학/재정학 분야에 대한 적용가능성 고찰

description:
포스테키안 핵심역량: 대인관계역량, 글로벌시민역량, 지식탐구역량, 자기관리역량
이 강의는 현대 사회를 살아가는 사람들이 직면하는 다양한 정신건강 문제를 이해하고, 이를 예방하고 효과적으로 대응하기 위한 기초적인 심리학 지식을 학습하는 것을 목표로 합니다. 특히 이상심리학의 과학적 기초를 바탕으로 정신장애의 주요 증상, 원인, 치료에 대해 이해함과 동시에, 정신건강의 회복과 향상이라는 인간적인 차원도 함께 조명합니다.
현대인의 삶은 다양한 스트레스 요인과 자기조절의 어려움 속에서 정신건강의 위협을 받고 있으며, 이에 대한 올바른 이해와 대응 능력은 개인의 삶의 질과 밀접하게 연결됩니다. 이 과목은 수강생들이 스트레스 관련 장애, 해리장애, 신체 증상 및 관련 장애, 기분장애와 자살, 중독장애, 섭식장애, 수면 각성 장애, 성생활과 관련된 장애, 조현병 스펙트럼 장애, 성격장애, 아동기와 청소년기의 이상행동, 신경인지장애와 노화 관련 장애 등 현대 사회에서 빈번하게 나타나는 정신장애의 특성과 원인을 학습하고, 이를 예방하거나 조기에 개입할 수 있는 다양한 상담 및 치료 접근법을 익힐 수 있도록 구성되어 있습니다.
또한, 정신장애를 경험하는 사람들의 회복과 재활에 대한 철학적 관점과 실천적 방법을 다루며, 정신건강을 증진시키는 건강한 생활양식, 자기조절 능력, 동기화된 삶의 태도를 함께 탐구합니다. 궁극적으로 이 수업은 수강생들이 자기 자신과 타인의 정신건강을 이해하고, 도울 수 있는 통합적 관점을 갖출 수 있도록 돕는 것을 목표로 합니다.

리딩 페이퍼는 정신재활, 정신병을 만드는 사람들, 정신의학의 역사, 몸이 아니라고 말할 때, 정상이라는 환상 중 한 권을 읽고 이상심리학에서 배운 내용을 토대로 생각한 바를 서술함. 페이퍼는 5페이지 이상 분량으로 하되 책의 내용을 요약하는 것

과서에서 배우는 이상행동과 관련 있거나 일치하는 영화, 다큐멘터리, 드라마, 유투브 동영상 등의 시청각 자료를 중심으로 15-20분 가량의 발표자료를 준비하여 수업시간에 발표하고 자료를 제출한다. 자료의 관련성, 독특성, 정확성등을 중심으로 평가한다

This course examines basic theoretical concepts and models underpinning the study of media communication, including processes of message construction in media organizations, content patterns, audience message processing, media effects, and media systems. Specific goals are as follows:

a. To increase your understanding of the role of media in the lives of individuals and society.
b. To enhance your awareness of how various media content affects your own and others’ attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors.
c. To increase your knowledge of media theories that explain and predict media choice and influence.
d. To assist you in developing digital media literacy skills and a critical understanding of how various forms of media function in your lives and in society.

course_operation:
[수강생 참고사항]
1. 과제는 마가렛 미드 및 나폴레옹 샤그농 논쟁에 관련된 본문 및 비평을 읽고 자신의 생각을 정리하는 것입니다. 얼마나 명쾌하게 글을 쓰는가, 글쓴이의 논지를 정확하게 이해하는가,자신의 주장에 대한 논거가 확실한가에 따라 평가합니다. 3주차에 과제에 대한 자세한 안내문이 배포될 것입니다.
2. 시험에는 객관식 (다지 선다형) 및 주관식 (서술형) 이 혼합되어 출제될 것입니다. 
3. 피치못할 사정으로 시험을 치르지 못하는 학생은 저와 미리 상의하고 사정을 증명하는 서류를 미리 제출하는 경우에 한해 시험 대신에 별도의 과제물을 부여할 것입니다.
4. 무단결석은 가장 첫 주(수강변경기간)을 제외하고 1번까지 할 수 있습니다. 두 번째의 결석부터는 출석점수에서 4점씩 감점이 있을 것입니다. 지각 두 번은 결석 한 번과 동일하게 처리합니다. 피치못할 사정으로 결석을 할 경우, 결석 다음 주에 그 사정을 증명하는 서류를 제출하여야 출석으로 인정됩니다. 2주가 지난 결석사유서는 받지 않을 것입니다.

description:

The focus of the course will be on the topics of pattern recognition, attention, memory, language, judgment making, and consciousness. We will also attempt to integrate some recent evidence from neuroscientific discoveries. By the end of this course, you should know a good deal about how cognition works, and also about the means to study it.

3. To develop the competencies of an effective and strategic communicator.

grading:
- Writing Assignment (Individual) — 30%
- Analysis of Persuasive Communication in Science Video Content (Group) — 30%
- Quizzes (4 times) — 30%
- Class Participation — 10%

* Absences: −0.5 points each; tardiness: −0.2 points each.
** No separate midterm or final exam will be held.

1. Writing Assignment (30%): A one-time exercise in which students work through a persuasion problem presented by the instructor. Students apply and extend course concepts to a new persuasion context of their own design.
**Task: Crafting effective and strategic messages for exerting influence in group, organizational, and interpersonal contexts.

2. Analysis of Persuasive Communication in Science Video Content (30%): Students will analyze the persuasive strategies used in popular science video content (e.g., YouTube channels). The analysis must explicitly draw on the theoretical models covered in class to evaluate how the content influences its audience. This group project will be carried out progressively throughout the semester, including a 1-page progress report and consultations. The final deliverable must be submitted and presented as a PowerPoint file.

3. Quizzes (30%): Designed to assess students' understanding of course concepts. A total of four quizzes will be administered throughout the semester.

4. Class Participation (10%): Regular and active attendance, along with completion and submission of various worksheets distributed by the instructor during class.
textbooks: Persuasion: Theory and Research (Daniel J. O'Keefe); The Dynamics of Persuasion (Richard M. Perloff)
references: Reading materials will be made available on PLMS throughout the semester.
course_operation:
1. Students will study persuasion topics (see the course schedule) grounded in social scientific research methods, primarily lab and field experiments involving human subjects. The course also reviews empirical studies that have tested various persuasion theories, with attention to how the "conclusions" drawn on different persuasion topics were actually arrived at. This course will be particularly useful for students interested in conducting usability tests with human subjects in the future.

2. Students will examine actual experimental studies on persuasion and practice critically engaging with their underlying assumptions, theoretical logic, methodology, and alternative interpretations of the findings.

3. This course will differ from what students might expect if they assume it covers the kind of self-help books on persuasion commonly found in bookstores (e.g., "secrets" or "tricks" of persuasion). Students should keep in mind that this course approaches persuasion from a scientific and ethical standpoint.

4. Persuasion is distinct from manipulation, propaganda, inducement, and coercion. This course focuses on persuasion grounded in an ethical approach.

5. The course consists of the instructor's lectures, quizzes, group presentations by students, discussions, and occasional in-class worksheets.

description:
Course Description

This course explores how people and the environment can interact in ways that support both sustainability and social well-being. Using real-world problems, students will learn tools and models from both the social and natural sciences to better understand these complex systems.

Part 1: Understanding the Basics
We start by learning a framework that helps us break down and analyze systems where people and nature are closely linked. Students will use basic mathematical models to explore how these systems change over time and what causes stability or sudden shifts. We’ll also study how people make decisions—individually and in groups—through simple game theory examples.

Part 2: Real-World Applications and Final Projects
Next, the class will focus on real-world challenges such as managing shared resources and promoting cooperation. From Weeks 12 to 15, students will lead discussions and explore how various social and environmental factors influence behavior and outcomes. At the same time, they will work on independent projects on a topic of their choice, using tools like MATLAB, Python, or XPPAUT. This process includes developing a proposal, receiving feedback, and presenting the final project at the end of the term. Final presentations and written reports may be completed in either Korean or English, depending on your preference.

Expected Learning outcomes
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
1. Analyze dynamic systems using one or more differential equations.
2. Formulate real-world problems and construct simplified models to investigate them.
3. Apply key concepts from the course to understand resilience, social-ecological systems, human behavior and governance, and infrastructure dynamics.

강의개요

이 강의는 인간과 환경이 어떻게 지속가능성과 사회적 후생을 모두 지원하는 방식으로 상호작용할 수 있는지를 탐구한다. 현실 세계의 문제들을 바탕으로, 학생들은 사회과학과 자연과학에서 사용되는 다양한 도구와 모델을 배우며 복잡한 시스템을 이해하는 능력을 탑재하게 될 것이다.

1부: 기본 개념 이해하기
인간과 자연이 밀접하게 연결된 시스템을 분해하고 분석할 수 있도록 돕는 하나의 분석틀을 배우는 것부터 시작한다. 학생들은 기본적인 수학 모델을 활용하여 이러한 시스템이 시간에 따라 어떻게 변화하는지, 그리고 어떤 요인이 안정성 또는 급격한 변화(전환)를 유발하는지를 살펴본다. 또한, 개인 및 집단 수준에서 사람들이 어떻게 의사결정을 내리는지를 간단한 게임이론 사례를 통해 배운다.

2부: 실제 사례 적용과 기말 프로젝트
이후 강의는 공유자원의 관리, 협력의 촉진 등 현실적인 문제 해결에 초점을 맞춘다. 12주차부터 15주차까지는 학생들의 참여와 토론을 통해 진행하며, 다양한 사회적 및 환경적 요인이 인간의 개별적 행태가 시스템 수준의 집합적 결과에 어떤 영향을 미치는지를 탐색한다. 이와 병행하여, 학생들은 각자의 관심 주제를 바탕으로 독립적인 프로젝트를 수행한다. MATLAB, Python, 또는 XPPAUT와 같은 도구를 활용하여 프로젝트를 진행하며, 이 프로젝트에는 제안서 작성, 피드백 세션 참여, 학기 말 최종 발표 및 기말페이퍼 제출까지 포함된다. 토론, 발표 및 기말페이퍼는 한국어로 진행해도 무방하다.

Lesson Objectives:
Course Description

This course explores how people and the environment can interact in ways that support both sustainability and social well-being. Using real-world problems, students will learn tools and models from both the social and natural sciences to better understand these complex systems.

Part 1: Understanding the Basics
We start by learning a framework that helps us break down and analyze systems where people and nature are closely linked. Students will use basic mathematical models to explore how these systems change over time and what causes stability or sudden shifts. We’ll also study how people make decisions—individually and in groups—through simple game theory examples.

Part 2: Real-World Applications and Final Projects
Next, the class will focus on real-world challenges such as managing shared resources and promoting cooperation. From Weeks 12 to 15, students will lead discussions and explore how various social and environmental factors influence behavior and outcomes. At the same time, they will work on independent projects on a topic of their choice, using tools like MATLAB, Python, or XPPAUT. This process includes developing a proposal, receiving feedback, and presenting the final project at the end of the term. Final presentations and written reports may be completed in either Korean or English, depending on your preference.

Expected Learning outcomes
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
1. Analyze dynamic systems using one or more differential equations.
2. Formulate real-world problems and construct simplified models to investigate them.
3. Apply key concepts from the course to understand resilience, social-ecological systems, human behavior and governance, and infrastructure dynamics.

Lecture progress plan:
1. Week 1 (9/1-9/5): Course Intro; IAD Framework
2. Week 2 (9/8-9/12): Stability analysis in 1-Dimension: Graphical Approach (Population dynamics); Non-dimensionalization in 1-D
3. Week 3 (9/15-9/19): Regime shifts/bifurcation (Resource-harvest dynamics); Resilience thinking
4. Week 4 (9/22-9/26): Stability analysis in 1-D: Formal approach; A model of forest-budworm outbreak dynamics; and Resilience thinking
5. Week 5 (9/29-10/3): Critical slowing down and Early warning signals of critical transitions; Resilience, Adaptability, & Transformability
6. Week 6 (10/6-10/10): Korean Thanksgiving Day and Hangul day (Tuesday and Thursday)
7. Week 7 (10/13-10/17): Stability analysis in 2-D: Graphical approach (Competition dynamics)
8. Week 8 (10/20-10/24): Midterm Exam Period (No midterm exam for this course)
9. Week 9 (10/27-10/31): Modeling social change (evolutionary game theory); Problem set #1; Quiz 1
10.	Week 10 (11/3-11/7): Modeling social change (evolutionary game theory); Modeling diffusion phenomena
11.	Week 11 (11/10-11/14): Stability analysis in 2-D: Formal approach; Problem set #2&3
12.	Week 12 (11/17-11/21): Short catch-up lectures and student-led discussions; Project proposal
13.	Week 13 (11/24-11/28): Project proposal; Proposal presentation
14.	Week 14 (12/1-12/5): Project consultation; Quiz 2
15.	Week 15 (12/8-12/12): Project presentation

grading:
- Problem-set assignments (35%)
- Quiz (10%)
- Model presentations (15%)
- Research project (40%): Each student will complete a dynamic modeling project based on their individual research interests. The project consists of three main components:
•	Proposal (7%): In the middle of the semester, you will deliver a brief presentation outlining your research question, modeling approach, and goals for the project.
•	Final Presentation (8%): During the final week, you will present your completed project to the class and engage in discussion about your findings and insights.
•	Project Report (25%): Your final report should follow the academic writing standards of your field. It should clearly state a research question, review relevant literature, describe the model, present a thorough analysis, and explain how the results address your research question.
Final presentations and written reports may be completed in either Korean or English, depending on your preference.

*HASS 교수는 WI 과제의 목적이 “해당 주제에 대해 일반대중을 합리적 근거를 통해 설득시키는 것”임을 고려하여 주제를 제시하고 이러한 목적을 학생들에게 주지시킨다.
*HASS 교수는 과제 부여 시, ‘주제’와 ‘취지/목적’ 그리고 (필요하다면) ‘필수 참고자료’를 WI 교수 및 WI 신청 학생들에게 제시한다.
*WI 교수는 ‘학술에세이 작성법’과 ‘평가기준’ 및 ‘과정별 과제 제출 일정’을 LMS에 미리 공지한다.
*WI 교수는 학술 에세이 과제에 대한 과정별 지도와 평가를 담당한다.
*WI 교수는 글쓰기 지도 과정에서, 완성된 글을 첨삭해 주는 데 초점을 맞추지 않고, 글쓰기의 과정에 따라 학생 스스로 글의 문제점을 발견하고 이를 직접 해결해 나갈 수 있도록 하는 데 중점을 둔다.
*WI 학술 에세이 분량: 한글 문서 기준 A4 3-4매. 제목, 이름, 차례, 참고자료를 제외한 본문만 해당 (글자 크기 10pt, 줄간격 160% *각주의 경우 글자 크기 9pt).

Students learn the fundamental concepts and principles of physics introduced in General Physics through laboratory experiments.
Students carry out a Design and Build project in which they design and construct their own experimental apparatus for a given topic and evaluate its performance. description: This PHYS250 is a laboratory course designed primarily for undergraduate students majoring in physics and engineering. You will do experiments and analyze the resulting data on a variety of topics taught in physics classes. You will perform a distinct experiment every week among the following topics. During the semester, you will learn how to write experimental reports.
prerequisites: 없음

You will do experiments and analyze the resulting data on a variety of topics taught in physics classes. You will perform a distinct experiment every week among the following topics. During the semester, you will learn how to write experimental reports.
Lecture progress plan:
1. Hysteresis curve for ferromagnetic material 
2. Electron motion in a magnetic field
3. Stefan-Boltzmann's law of radiation

grading:
30% Prelab quiz + 60% 보고서 + 10% 발표
1. Prelab quiz: 실험 매뉴얼 숙지. 실험 전 실험 내용 및 방법에 관한 퀴즈 진행 (2문제, 문제 당 15점)

2. 보고서: PLMS에 업로드 된 채점기준을 확인하여 보고서 작성. 보고서 제출 기한 일주일 (수/금요일 분반의 경우, 실험을 수행한 주와 해당 실험의 보충 실험 주가 끝나는 다음 주 수/금요일 23:59 까지). 제출마감 이후 제출 시 하루 당 20% 감점. 보고서 형식은 LaTex 사용 권장. MS word로 작성 시 PDF 파일로 변환 후 제출. 보고서 양식은 PLMS에 업로드 된 안내 참조.

3. 발표: 6개의 실험 중 자율적으로 하나를 선택하여 10분간 발표 + 2-3 분 정도의 질의응답 시간. 평가는 조교 평가 + 동료 평가로 합산된 점수에 의해 총점 결정됨. 평가의 모든 참여 인원이 발표자에 대해 0~10 점 사이의 점수를 입력하고 평균 점수가 최종 발표 점수가 됨.

description: The basic unit of information in computing and digital communications is the bit or the binary digit. The bit is commonly expressed with binary values 0 and 1, which represent the classical physical state of a two-state system; off/on, low/high, etc. The bit-based information processing and communication is called classical information. In quantum information, information is encoded in the state of a two-level quantum system. As a key feature of a quantum system is quantum superposition, quantum information is represented by a quantum bit or a qubit whose state can be written as |ψ⟩=α|0⟩+β|1〉. Moreover, multiple qubits may exhibit entanglement, a unique quantum phenomenon. By taking advantage of superposition and entanglement, quantum information processing enables computing and communication paradigms that are not available in classical information. Experimental quantum information requires extremely accurate and precise control of multi-qubit quantum states and is an intense subject of recent research. This class will focus on introducing basic concepts of quantum information science.
prerequisites: Quantum physics
Lesson Objectives: The basic unit of information in computing and digital communications is the bit or the binary digit. The bit is commonly expressed with binary values 0 and 1, which represent the classical physical state of a two-state system; off/on, low/high, etc. The bit-based information processing and communication is called classical information. In quantum information, information is encoded in the state of a two-level quantum system. As a key feature of a quantum system is quantum superposition, quantum information is represented by a quantum bit or a qubit whose state can be written as |ψ⟩=α|0⟩+β|1〉. Moreover, multiple qubits may exhibit entanglement, a unique quantum phenomenon. By taking advantage of superposition and entanglement, quantum information processing enables computing and communication paradigms that are not available in classical information. Experimental quantum information requires extremely accurate and precise control of multi-qubit quantum states and is an intense subject of recent research. This class will focus on introducing basic concepts of quantum information science.
Lecture progress plan:
Topics to be covered (tentative)
# Quantum physics vs classical physics
- Stern Gerlach experiment and quantum superposition
- Quantum measurement (what is spin half?)
- Local realism, uncertainty principle, and Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen "paradox"
- Bell's inequality
- Meaning of Bell's inequality violation

# Quantum state
- Pure state vs mixed state
- density matrix 
- reduced density matrix and sub-systems
- quantum measurement formalism

# Entanglement
- two-qubit entanglement
- entanglement vs classical correlation
- Bell states and Bell basis
- non-maximally entangled pure states
- Werner states
- decoherence 
- maximally entangled mixed states
- entanglement sudden death
- quantifying purity and entanglement (entropy, concurrence, discord, steering)
- separability and negative partial transpose
- non-physical quantum operations
- LOCC and entanglement purification

# Quantum measurement
- Distinguishing orthogonal states
- Distinguishing non-orthogonal states
- POVM
- weak measurement and weak values

# Multipartite and/or multidimensional entanglement
- Bound entanglement
- GHZ state
- W state
- Entanglement witness

# Quantum information processing (very quickly)
- Channel capacity and Holevo bound
- Dense coding and Teleportation
- quantum cryptography
- simple quantum algorithms
- decoherence, quantum error, fault tolerance
- Fisher information
- Heisenberg limit

description:
In this course, we aim to cover :
1) the mathematical language of quantum information processing: density matrices, measurements, channels, etc.
2) the basics of circuit based quantum computing: qubits, single-/two-qubit gates, simple quantum algorithms
3) leading quantum computing hardware platforms: neutral atoms, superconducting circuits, etc. - coherence, fidelity, connectivity, scaling, benchmarking
4) core problems in quantum simulation: many-body quantum simulation (Hubbard models, spin models), analog vs. digital (Trotterization, Jordan-Wigner transformation), VQE and quantum chemistry, etc.

description:
- Understand the framework of quantum information theory.
- Understand basic quantum information protocols.
- Understand key quantum information-theoretic quantities
- Understand the basic principles of quantum algorithms and NISQ algorithms.
- Understand the fundamentals of quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computation.
- Read, discuss, and present recent research papers in quantum information theory and related areas.
prerequisites: Quantum mechanics, Linear algebra
Lesson Objectives:
- Understand the framework of quantum information theory.
- Understand basic quantum information protocols.
- Understand key quantum information-theoretic quantities
- Understand the basic principles of quantum algorithms and NISQ algorithms.
- Understand the fundamentals of quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computation.
- Read, discuss, and present recent research papers in quantum information theory and related areas.
Lecture progress plan:
[Part1 (6 weeks)]
1. Basic of Quantum Information Theory 
- Pure and mixed states
- Quantum measurements
- Composite Systems and Entanglement
- No-cloning theorem 
- Bell theorem 
2, Basic Quantum Information Protocols
- Single-qubit and multi-qubit gates, universal gate sets
- Quantum teleportation and superdense coding
- Entanglement swapping and quantum repeaters
- Entanglement distillation and purification
- Quantum key distribution and quantum secret sharing 
3. Quantum Channels and Quantum Entropy
- CPTP maps and Kraus representations
- Basic quantum noise channels
- von Neumann entropy, mutual information, relative entropy
- Holevo bound and channel capacity

[Part2 (6 weeks)]
4. Introduction to Quantum Algorithms
- Oracle model and quantum interference
- Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm
- Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm
- Simon’s algorithm 
- Grover’s algorithm and amplitude amplification
- Quantum Fourier transform
- Phase estimation algorithm
- Shor’s algorithm
5. NISQ Algorithms
- NISQ devices and their limitations
- Variational Quantum Eigensolver
- Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
- Parameterized quantum circuits and barren plateaus
- Digital Hamiltonian simulation and Trotterization
- Quantum error mitigation
6. Quantum Error Correction and Fault Tolerance
- Quantum noise and decoherence
- Basic quantum error-correcting codes
- Stabilizer formalism
- Surface code and fault-tolerant quantum computation

[Part3 (2~3 weeks)]
Project-based seminar on recent research topics
- Individual projects.
- Topic selection based on quantum information theory and related areas
- Literature review of selected research papers or small research projects.
- Focus on main ideas, technical methods, significance, limitations, and future directions.
- Oral presentation and short final report.
grading:
- Homework : 40%
- Final Project : 40%
- Attendance : 20%

course_operation:
Course Overview & Teaching Methodology

This course is built on traditional theoretical rigor, active problem-solving, and modern computational visualization:

Blackboard Talk & Python Demos: Lectures are delivered on the blackboard to build a deep, step-by-step understanding of mathematical derivations and physical intuition. Wednesday classes complement these lectures with interactive Python demonstrations to visualize quantum mechanical phenomena.

Homework & Bi-Weekly Quizzes: Ungraded weekly homework problems from McQuarrie’s textbook serve as your primary study guide. Understanding these problems is key, as bi-weekly 25-minute quizzes are directly adapted from homework assignments.

Student-Led Presentations: Starting after the midterm, students take the chalk during the second half of Wednesday classes to lead concise, 10-minute blackboard presentations on specific derivations and physical mechanisms.

description: This course introduces the fundamental principles of biochemistry, with an emphasis on understanding the relationships among molecular structure, chemical interactions, and biological function. Students will develop the ability to apply these principles to understand biochemical mechanisms and interpret experimental data, while connecting fundamental concepts to contemporary research.
prerequisites: A basic understanding of general chemistry and organic chemistry is recommended. Prior coursework in biology is helpful but not required.
Lesson Objectives: This course introduces the fundamental principles of biochemistry, with an emphasis on understanding the relationships among molecular structure, chemical interactions, and biological function. Students will develop the ability to apply these principles to understand biochemical mechanisms and interpret experimental data, while connecting fundamental concepts to contemporary research.
Lecture progress plan:
Week 1. Biochemistry: An Evolving Science
Week 2. Protein Structure and Function
Week 3. Exploring Proteins and Proteomes
Week 4. Enzymes: Kinetics and Catalysis
Week 5. Enzyme Regulation and Allostery
Week 6. Lipids, Membranes, Channels, and Pumps
Week 7. DNA, RNA, and the Flow of Genetic Information
Week 8. Midterm Examination
Week 9. Bioenergetics and the Logic of Metabolism
Week 10. Glucose Metabolism: Glycolysis, Gluconeogenesis, and Glycogen
Week 11. Citric Acid Cycle and Oxidative Phosphorylation
Week 12. Metabolic Integration and Fuel Metabolism
Week 13. Signal Transduction
Week 14. Frontiers in Molecular and Membrane Biochemistry
Week 15. From Molecular Mechanism to Discovery
Week 16. Final Examination
grading:
Midterm Examination 35%
Final Examination 35%
Participation & Discussion 25%
Attendance 5%
textbooks: Biochemistry, 8-10th Edition. (erg, J. M., Tymoczko, J. L., Gatto, G. J., Jr., and Stryer, L.)

Additional lecture materials, selected research articles, structural and biochemical data, and other supplementary resources will be provided throughout the course when appropriate.
course_operation: This course will combine lectures with problem solving, discussion, and interpretation of biochemical and structural data. Fundamental biochemical concepts will be introduced through lectures and progressively connected to experimental observations and contemporary research. In the later part of the course, students will apply these concepts to analyze molecular mechanisms and research questions.
other_info: Lecture notes and related materials will be uploaded to e-Class before each class. Students are encouraged to review the lecture materials in advance. Selected biochemical problems, molecular structures, and research figures may be discussed during class. Active participation and scientific discussion are encouraged.

course_operation: This is a graduate level course but I strongly recommend senior undergraduate students to take this class, who especially are interested in synthetic chemistry. This class will cover basic inorganic/organometallic chemistry with emphasis on the understanding of reaction kinetics/mechanisms using a practical computation program as well as other basic spectroscopic information. The first half of the class (before Week 8) will be individual trainings for students to be familiar with computation. Therefore, students will be asked to bring their personal laptops in the class.  As I teach the computation on a person-to-person basis, class attendance will be one of the most important factors to evaluate students. Only pre-approved absence will be allowed. Limited students can audit the class due to the computing resources (computer clusters).
other_info: The lecture will be given in English.

course_operation:
Do not miss the class. Unapproved absence of more than 5 times will result in course failure. I found the correlation between the number of absence and grade is very close to 1. Doing homework is essential. You should do it to your best. Homework grade is based on how hard you worked on it. Some problem sets may require using math programs such as Matlab. The lecture will be given in English
   You are encouraged to study together and to discuss information and concepts covered in lecture with other students. You can give "consulting" help to or receive "consulting" help from such students. However, this permissible cooperation should never involve one student having possession of a copy of all or part of work done by someone else. Should copying occur, both the student who copied work from another student and the student who gave material to be copied will automatically receive a zero for the assignment. Penalty for violation of this Code can also be extended to include failure of the course and University disciplinary action.

Triggered by recent development of optical technologies, a number of unprecedented imaging methods are available now. In addition to imaging itself, a new powerful methodogy that takes advantage of existing methods recently emerges, optogentics. It would allow us to modulate a number of physiological features at the cellular level and also organism level, which can be potetially applicable to various approaches such as neuroscience. This lecture has been devised for students to understand principles of microscopes and learn about a variety of new molecular imaging methods, incluidng the recent application such as optogenetics.

description: The course is designed to introduce important concepts, methods, and tools of Bioinformatics. Topics include (but not limited to) sequence comparison and alignment, databases and data formats, phylogenetic analysis, gene prediction and regulation, prediction of deleterious amino acid substitutions, Protein Classification, Protein structure prediction such as alphafold, protein-protein Interactions, membrane protein structures. Emphasis will be put on the understanding and utilization of these concepts and algorithms. The objective is to help the students to understand the key concepts of bioinformatics and be able to use the bioinformatics tools to solve the problems on their own research.
Lesson Objectives: The course is designed to introduce important concepts, methods, and tools of Bioinformatics. Topics include (but not limited to) sequence comparison and alignment, databases and data formats, phylogenetic analysis, gene prediction and regulation, prediction of deleterious amino acid substitutions, Protein Classification, Protein structure prediction such as alphafold, protein-protein Interactions, membrane protein structures. Emphasis will be put on the understanding and utilization of these concepts and algorithms. The objective is to help the students to understand the key concepts of bioinformatics and be able to use the bioinformatics tools to solve the problems on their own research.
Lecture progress plan:
1. Introduction and Overview
2. DNA sequence variation (polymorphism and deleterious amino acid substitutions)
3. Gene expression (Gene prediction and regulation)
4. Subcellular localization (Trafficking and target signaling)
5. Protein modification (phosphorylation prediction)
6.  Protein structure (prediction and design)
7. Protein-protein interaction (recognition, sorting, interactome, docking, networking)
8. Protein-DNA (RNA) interaction (aptamer, nucleotide structure prediction)
9. Cell-Cell communication (signal transduction modules and membrane proteins)
10. Evolution (phylogenetic analysis, sequence conservation scoring, evolution coupling)
11.  Bio-patterns and motifs (search, comparison)
grading: Proposal writing, Presentations, and an exam

본 과목은 생명과학 및 생명공학 전공 학생들이 학계에 머무르지 않고, 글로벌 바이오산업의 현황과 미래 트렌드를 거시적으로 조망할 수 있도록 돕는 교과목입니다. 매주 바이오·제약 및 헬스케어 산업 최전선에서 활약 중인 기업 대표, 연구소장, 투자 전문가 등을 초빙하여 글로벌 시장을 흔들고 있는 핵심 플랫폼 기술과 비즈니스 모델을 학습합니다.

description: This course covers the fundamentals of thermodynamics for materials science and engineering chiefly based on the classical thermodynamics approach. The lecture begins with the definition of unique terminologies in thermodynamics like system, surrounding, property, state, equilibrium, etc. and then introduces some basic laws (the first, second, and third law) of thermodynamics including the concept of internal energy, enthalpy and entropy. Next, the basic criterion for phase equilibrium is established with the Gibbs free energy derived with the Legendre transformation of energy conservation equation. This concept extends to binary component system and finally provides the conceptual basis to understand a phase diagram. A fundamental electrochemistry can be introduced briefly at the end of class.

description: Macromolecular science has had a major impact on the way we live. It is difficult to find an aspect of our lives that is not affected by polymers. description: This course covers the fundamentals of electrochemistry for materials science and engineering including some important practical applications in energy research area. The lecture begins with an overview of electrode processes showing the way in which the fundamental components of the subject come together in an electrochemical experiment. Then, basic concepts of electrochemistry will be covered such as thermodynamics and potential, electron-transfer kinetics, and mass transfer. The basic concepts are integrated together in treatments of the various practical electrochemical methodologies. Finally, a few important applications of electrochemistry in materials science and engineering discipline will be briefly introduced such as batteries, fuel cells, water electrolysis, corrosion/anti-corrosion and electroplating.

description: This course introduces the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics and their application to light–matter interactions in gases and solids. Topics include the Schrödinger equation, perturbation theory, absorption and emission processes, interband transitions in semiconductors, exciton dynamics, and lattice vibrations. Emphasis is placed on developing both conceptual understanding and quantitative tools for analyzing optical phenomena in atomic and condensed-matter systems. The course provides a foundation for advanced study in quantum optics, semiconductor physics, and quantum materials.

description: In this class, we reviews the principles in Newtonian mechanics and extend them such that we could solve many applied dynamics problems in mechanical engineering. We will treat the Newton's Laws of motion such that they can be easily used in the three dimensional space even with respect to a non-inertial reference frame. Students will study the basics in the kinematics and kinetics of a particle, a system of particles, and rigid bodies. The basics of Lagrangian dynamics will be introduced for easier formulations of some complicated dynamics problems. Typical application cases of dynamics will be treated in mechanical engineering such as the velocity and acceleration, impulse and momentum, work and energy of some components in cam systems, rotating systems as gears, and rotors.

description:
In mechanical vibration class, we study the theory on the vibratory responses of a structure. The processes to learn about the characteristics of vibration of a structure may start with the study on the vibratory responses of a single-degree-of-freedom structure (or system) and continue to learn on the responses of muti-degree-of-freedom ones. Modeling of a structure as a vibration system may be considered simultaneously with the theoretical study on vibrations.

description:
This course covers manufacturing processes with material properties and design requirements taken into account. Processes studied include casting, bulk deformation, sheet-metal forming, powder-metal and ceramic processing, polymer processing, additive manufacturing, machining and finishing, advanced machining, and joining. The course also introduces engineering metrology, geometric dimensioning and tolerancing, and statistical process control, and closes with a framework for process selection, manufacturing cost, and sustainable manufacturing.

Learning outcomes- on completion, students should be able to:
1. Explain the physical principles, capabilities, and limitations of the major manufacturing process families.
2. Relate material properties and part geometry to process feasibility, defects, and achievable tolerances and surface finish.
3. Select an appropriate joining process and design a joint for a given material combination and service condition.
4. Interpret measurement data and tolerances (GD&T) and apply basic statistical process control.
5. Compare candidate processes for a given product on the basis of quality, rate, cost, and sustainability, and justify a selection.

description:
An electrical double layer (EDL) may appear at the interface between a fluid and an object (a solid or another immiscible fluid) in contact with each other. Upon the application of an electric field to this system, ions can experience an electromagnetic force, inducing fluid flow (e.g., electroosmotic flow) or causing  particles suspended within the fluid to migrate (e.g., electrophoresis). Electrokinetics is the discipline that addresses these phenomena and is a commonly utilized method for the manipulation of particles and fluids at the micro-to-nanometer scale.
Furthermore, when an electric potential is applied to electrodes submerged in a fluid, an electrical double layer forms on the electrode surfaces, leading to a phenomenon known as electrode polarization. This phenomenon not only profoundly impacts the monitoring and detection of biochemical reactions through electrical means but also generates various forms of fluid motion.
This course will cover the fundamental theories and knowledge of the electrical double layer and electrokinetics.

description:
This course introduces the classification, structure, reactions, and reaction mechanisms of organic compounds.

By the end of the course, students will be able to understand and apply concepts related to the classification, structure, nomenclature, reactions, reaction mechanisms, and synthesis of key organic compounds, including halocarbons, alkenes, and alcohols.

This foundation in the fundamentals of organic chemistry will support further study in organic synthesis, biochemistry, molecular biology, polymers, and their practical applications.

This foundation in the fundamentals of organic chemistry will support further study in organic synthesis, biochemistry, molecular biology, polymers, and their practical applications.

description:
Acquire knowledge about the physical and chemical properties of substances through experiments.
(물질의 물리화학적 특성에 대한 지식을 실험을 통해 익힌다.)
prerequisites:
Students must take the physical chemistry course as a prerequisite.
(물리화학 강의를 들어야 함.)
Lesson Objectives:
Acquire knowledge about the physical and chemical properties of substances through experiments.
(물질의 물리화학적 특성에 대한 지식을 실험을 통해 익힌다.)
Lecture progress plan:
1st week : orientation, lab group formation (오리엔테이션, 실험조 편성)
2nd week : Sputtering, freezing point depression of electrolyte solution (Sputtering , 전해질 용액의 어는점 내림)
3rd week : Gas-liquid equilibrium in a three-component system (이성분계에서의 기체-액체 평형)
4th week: Osmotic pressure measurement, conductivity measurement of electrolyte solutions (삼투압 측정, 전해질 용액의 전도도 측정)
5th week : Viscosity measurement of polymer solutions (고분자 용액의 점도 측정)
6th week : Vapor pressure measurement, surface tension (증기압 측정, 표면장력)
7th week : Bomb calorimeter, calorimetry method (Bomb 열량계, 열량계법)
8th week Midterm test period (중간고사 기간)
9th week : chemical reaction rate (화학반응속도)
10th week : ion transport rate (이온 운반율)
11th week : Festival (해맞이 한마당 축제)
12th week : Optical Interferometry, Electron & Optical Diffraction (광학 간섭계, 전자 & 광 회절)
13th week : Potentiometric titration using a pH meter (pH meter를 이용한 전위차 적정법)
14th week : liquid adsorption (액체흡착)
15th week : Vibrational spectrum of HCl-DCl (HCl-DCl의 회절-진동 스펙트럼)
16th week : Final test period (기말고사 기간)

description:
This course introduces the fundamental theories of numerical analysis, data analysis, and artificial intelligence, which are actively used in various fields of chemical engineering. It also aims to develop the ability to directly program related software using Python and to understand how these techniques are applied in major areas of chemical engineering.

The course is structured into four main parts:
(1) Introduction to Python: A basic introduction to the Python language and an overview of Python libraries widely used in mathematics, science, and engineering.
(2) Numerical Computing: An introduction to numerical analysis methods commonly used in chemical engineering and AI, with hands-on programming of numerical tools using Python.
(3) AI Algorithm Basics: A presentation of fundamental theories related to artificial intelligence, along with simple AI model programming using PyTorch.
(4) Applications of AI in Chemical Engineering: A review of specific examples of how artificial intelligence is being applied in the field of chemical engineering.

description: Colloid and interfacial phenomena play a central role in many industrial, environmental, and biomedical areas, as well as in emerging technologies. These include detergency, emulsification, and wetting; enhanced oil recovery and other petrochemical processes; personal care products; drug delivery systems; thin films; and microfabrication of electronic and electro-optic devices. CHEB313 is intended to provide an introduction to theoretical, experimental, and applied aspects of colloidal systems, as well as interfacial phenomena.

CHEB313 is intended to provide an introduction to theoretical, experimental, and applied aspects of colloidal systems, as well as interfacial phenomena.

description:
Almost everything that defines this decade, including AI datacenters, phone cameras, solar cells, memory chips, 
comes down to a single question: what do electrons do inside a material? 
This course teaches you to answer it.

1. Structure → Electronic states 
View a material's atomic arrangement and predict the electronic states it gives rise to.
2. Band structure → Properties
Use electronic band structures to explain why a material conducts, insulates, absorbs, or emits light.
3. From silicon to nanomaterials 
Compare the electrical and optical behavior of real semiconductors, from silicon crystals to emerging nanomaterials.
4. Devices 
Work out how the IT, ET, and NT devices around you (ex. transistors, image sensors, light-emitting devices, memories) actually operate.

description:
(Approximately half of this course will be delivered by invited external experts. Therefore, we kindly ask for your understanding that a significant portion of the lectures will be conducted in Korean.)

Significant efforts have been dedicated to developing and improving new materials for lithium-ion batteries to meet the growing power and energy demands of mobile electronics and electric vehicles. However, the widespread adoption of large-format lithium-ion batteries remains limited due to high costs, safety concerns, and limitations in energy density and calendar life. Advanced materials processing techniques offer promising solutions to these challenges.

This course provides a comprehensive overview of key materials processing methods used in the fabrication of cathodes, anodes, and separators for lithium-ion batteries. To cultivate specialized professionals in the field of secondary batteries and reflect the needs of industry, the curriculum goes beyond basic principles to include instruction on battery materials, synthesis strategies, and cell assembly. In line with the goals of the Graduate Program for Battery-Specialized Universities, the course is designed to foster highly trained battery professionals by covering topics ranging from the fundamentals of secondary batteries to seminar programs delivered by experts actively working in academia and industry. Additionally, guest lectures (in Korean) by leading experts from academia and industry will offer insights into current issues and real-world practices in Korea’s secondary battery sector.
prerequisites:
[This course is designed for new graduate students or undergraduate students. Students who are already conducting research on secondary batteries are advised to take a different course]

This course provides a comprehensive overview of key materials processing methods used in the fabrication of cathodes, anodes, and separators for lithium-ion batteries. To cultivate specialized professionals in the field of secondary batteries and reflect the needs of industry, the curriculum goes beyond basic principles to include instruction on battery materials, synthesis strategies, and cell assembly. In line with the goals of the Graduate Program for Battery-Specialized Universities, the course is designed to foster highly trained battery professionals by covering topics ranging from the fundamentals of secondary batteries to seminar programs delivered by experts actively working in academia and industry. Additionally, guest lectures (in Korean) by leading experts from academia and industry will offer insights into current issues and real-world practices in Korea’s secondary battery sector.
Lecture progress plan:
•	Week 1: Introduction to Lithium-Ion Battery
•	Week 2: Electrochemistry Basics: Electricity, Chemistry
•	Week 3: Electrochemistry Basics: Electromotive force, Electric Current
•	Week 4: Lithium-Ion Battery Operation 1
•	Week 5: Lithium-Ion Battery Operation 2
•	Week 6: Overview and Comparison of Different Lithium-ion Chemistry
•	Week 7: The Cathodes
•	Week 8: The Anodes
•	Week 9: Inactive Materials: Binders, Electrolytes
•	Week 10: Inactive Materials: Separators, Current Collectors 
•	Week 11: Raw Materials and Recycling
•	Week 12: Lithium-ion Cell Manufacturing 1
•	Week 13: Lithium-ion Cell Manufacturing 2
•	Week 14: Next Generation and beyond lithium chemistries 2
•	Week 15: The Future and Energy Storage

description:
[Course Overview]
With the increasing significance of eco-friendly energy materials, there is a growing demand for a convergent understanding of analytical techniques to characterize materials and elucidate the mechanisms behind performance enhancement. Given the rising complexity of modern materials, an in-depth understanding through multi-dimensional analysis is essential. Accordingly, this course introduces undergraduate students in Chemical Engineering and related convergent disciplines to the current development of various energy materials and the practical application of characterization tools, focusing on their fundamental principles and operational scopes.

[Learning Objectives]
- Fundamental Principles: Grasp the core principles of various analytical techniques utilized for characterizing energy and environmental materials, specifically for hydrogen production, storage, extraction, utilization, and CO2 reduction.
- Technical Selection: Evaluate the strengths, limitations, and application ranges of each characterization method to select the most appropriate tools for specific research objectives.
- Integrated Interpretation: Develop the ability to synthesize diverse analytical datasets to achieve a profound understanding of material properties within the hydrogen economy and carbon capture frameworks.

description: To explore the principles and applications of silicon-based electronic systems interfacing with biological environments, with a focus on biosensors, neural interfaces, lab-on-a-chip systems, and neuromorphic devices.
prerequisites: Electrochemistry for Chemical Engineering (특강: 화공전기화학) 을 수강하면 듣기 수월합니다.
Lesson Objectives: To explore the principles and applications of silicon-based electronic systems interfacing with biological environments, with a focus on biosensors, neural interfaces, lab-on-a-chip systems, and neuromorphic devices.
Lecture progress plan:
Week 1: Introduction & Course Overview
  Course goals, structure, and grading
  What is Si-bio interface engineering?
  Overview of application areas: biosensing, neural interfaces, lab-on-a-chip, neuromorphic devices

Week 2: Basics of Electronic Materials
  Semiconductor fundamentals (Si, PN junctions, doping)
  Conductors, insulators, semiconductors
  Introduction to the MOS structure

Week 3: Micro/Nano Fabrication Techniques
  Introduction to cleanroom processes (photolithography, etching, deposition)
  CMOS-compatible fabrication
  Fabrication strategies for bio-integrated systems

Week 4: Fundamentals of Circuits and Sensors
  Basic circuit elements (resistors, capacitors, op-amps)
  Analog vs. digital signals
  Common circuit designs for biosignal acquisition

Week 5: Understanding Bioelectrical Signals
  Types of biological electrical signals (EEG, ECG, action potentials)
  Physiological origin of electrical signals
  Signal-to-noise challenges in bioelectronics

Week 6: Basics of Bioelectronic Interfaces
  Electrochemical interfaces: electrode-cell interactions
  Electric double layer, impedance, charge injection
  Electrode materials: Au, Pt, PEDOT:PSS, etc.

Week 7: Biosensors I – Electrochemical Sensing
  Potentiometric, amperometric, and conductometric sensors
  Electrolyte–insulator–semiconductor (EIS) structures
  Applications: DNA sensing, protein detection

Week 8: Biosensors II – FET-based Biosensors
  ISFET, BioFET, Graphene FETs
  Strategies to improve sensitivity and selectivity
  Applications in bacterial and viral detection

Week 9: Neural Interfaces I – Recording Neuronal Signals
  Basics of microelectrode arrays (MEAs)
  Intracellular vs. extracellular signal acquisition
  Engineering challenges in neuron-electrode interfaces

Week 10: Neural Interfaces II – Stimulation & Electroceuticals
  Methods of electrical stimulation
  Introduction to electroceuticals
  Brain stimulation and neuromodulation case studies

Week 11: Lab-on-a-Chip & Organ-on-a-Chip Systems
  Basics of microfluidics
  Design and applications of biochips
  Diagnostic chips and cell-culture systems

Week 12: Neuromorphic Devices & Artificial Synapses
  Memristors, IGZO, phase-change memories
  Comparison to biological synapses
  Neuromorphic circuits and learning architectures

Week 13: Emerging Technologies in Bioelectronics
  Flexible and wearable biosensors
  Nanobiosensors (e.g., DNA origami, aptamer sensors)
  Bioelectronics in artificial organ development

Week 14: Final Project Preparation
  Project review and feedback
  Design revisions and finalization

Week 15: Final Presentations & Discussion
  Student presentations with Q&A
  Discussion on future trends and real-world applications
  Career paths in bioelectronics and interface engineering

description: The course focuses on interfacial thermodynamics, covering the enthalpy and entropy of adsorption and mixing between key materials. Students will learn the theoretical basis for predicting adsorption and desorption behavior using interfacial energy and explore various techniques for measuring surface energy. The course also addresses phase behavior in mixed solutions based on the physicochemical properties of surfactants. Finally, students will study junction properties between major electronic and optoelectronic materials.

description:
This class aims to comprehend the advanced principles and applications of solid catalysts and extend to the practical heterogeneous catalysis researches. From the fundamentals of adsorption on surfaces, this course covers the heterogeneous catalyst kinetics of surface reactions and energetics of catalytic materials, and several practical characterization tools are studied and utilized for the advanced solid catalysts researches. 
Together with some background knowledge for energy conversion chemistry and applications that have highly interdisciplinary nature, it shows the wide areas of most relevant scientific and technical aspects such as energy & environment, thermodynamics, kinetics of electrochemical reactions, and materials of electrode catalysts together with the state-of-the-art applications.
This class also covers the pivotal principles and applications of solid state electrochemistry with solid electrode materials and electrolytes, studying the backgrounds of ionics, electrodics, solid state electrolyte and electrode materials, some experimental techniques, and electrochemical devices for the highly advanced researchers working in the relevant research area. Some energy materials characterizations and their applications to recent energy storage devices such as  Li ion batteries, Li metal batteries, Li-S batteries will be introduced with the state-of-the-art techniques.

description: This course examines the critical environmental challenges shaping the Earth today. description:
Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with one another and with their physical environment. Although the definition of ecology appears rather simple, it comes with a deep history of how we have begun to organize living organisms at various biological levels (genetic, individual, population, community, ecosystem). It also comes with fundamental theories used to explain how different types of organisms come to adapt, survive, and co-exist in our environment. These theories, still to this date, are used to interpret historical, present, and future organizations and interactions between biota and environment.

The field of ecology has grown over the recent years, and it is now considered one of the most interdisciplinary research topics. The most notable branches of traditional ecology are “geoecology”, “ecological engineering”, and “human ecology”. Clearly, we have stepped out of the fundamental interactions between biota and environment—we are now altering ecological processes to design engineered ecosystems for various industrial and remediation purposes, and generating new theories to better describe how humans have organized themselves in the natural and social environment. 

In the first part of this course, we are going learn about the fundamental theories of ecology. In the second part of this course, we will learn about how humans have come to play in the conventional biota-environment interactions by exposing ourselves into interdisciplinary topics of geoecology, ecological engineering, and human ecology.

description: This graduate-level course explores the mechanical behavior of emerging metallic systems—including high-entropy alloys (HEAs), heterostructured materials, and other advanced alloys—through the lens of dislocation theory and microstructural design. Students will gain a theoretical foundation in dislocation mechanics and apply these principles to understand strengthening mechanisms, deformation behavior, and design strategies in cutting-edge metallic materials.
prerequisites:
• Undergraduate-level knowledge of materials science and mechanical behavior of materials
• Basic understanding of crystallography and physical metallurgy
Lesson Objectives: This graduate-level course explores the mechanical behavior of emerging metallic systems—including high-entropy alloys (HEAs), heterostructured materials, and other advanced alloys—through the lens of dislocation theory and microstructural design. Students will gain a theoretical foundation in dislocation mechanics and apply these principles to understand strengthening mechanisms, deformation behavior, and design strategies in cutting-edge metallic materials.
Lecture progress plan:
Week-by-Week Syllabus
Week	Topic	Key References / Reading
1-3	Introduction to Advanced Metallic Materials
Overview of HEAs, metastability, heterostructures	Gao et al., HEA: Fundamentals and Applications (Ch.1)
4	Strengthening Mechanisms in Metals
Grain boundaries, solid solution, precipitates	Meyers & Chawla (Ch.5–6), Murty et al. (Ch.4–5)
5	Solid Solution and Lattice Distortion in HEAs	Gao et al. (Ch.4), Selected Acta Mater. papers
6	Stacking Fault Energy and Planar Slip Behavior in HEAs	Selected journal articles, Discussion on SFE
7	Heterostructured Materials: Concepts and Microstructures	Wu et al., Heterostructured Materials (Ch.1–2)
8	HDI Strengthening and Strain Gradient Effects	Wu et al. (Ch.3–4), Selected IJPlasticity articles
9-11	Deformation Mechanisms in Dual-Phase and TRIP-Assisted HEAs	Recent literature reviews and case studies
12	Modeling Approaches: From Dislocation Dynamics to Crystal Plasticity	Introduction to CP-FEM
13	Design Principles for Next-Generation Alloys	Integrated materials design, CALPHAD, ML intro
14	Student Presentations: Recent Research Topics	Selected topics by students
15	Final Project Presentations and Discussions	Comprehensive review & wrap-up
grading:
Student performance will be assessed based on the following components:
•	Homework Assignments (Problem Sets and Short Essays) – 20%
Focused on key theoretical concepts and interpretation of experimental data.
•	Midterm Report (Literature Review) – 20%
Students will prepare a detailed literature review on a selected topic related to HEAs, dislocation theory, or heterostructured materials.
•	Class Presentation – 20%
Each student will present a recent research paper (published within the last 3 years) and lead a short discussion.
•	Final Project (Research Proposal or Case Study) – 40%
Students will develop a proposal or an in-depth case study involving mechanical behavior analysis, supported by theoretical or simulation-based interpretation.

description: This course is designed for the senior undergraduate and the graduate students of nuclear science, nuclear engineering, environmental science and engineering, biology, geology, and chemistry to provide an overview of fundamentals of radioactive waste management.  This course includes nuclear fuel cycle (front – and back-end), radioactive wastes generation and types, radiation source/measurement/effects/nuclear waste incineration, actinide chemistry, mechanisms of microbiological effects on radionuclide immobilization in the environment, treatment technology of radioactive wastes, waste form development and testing methods, geological storage and disposal of wastes, modeling of radionuclide transport, decontamination/decommissioning methods, and risk assessment/safe analysis of repository.  The primary goal of this course is to provide the students for understanding of radioactive wastes, immobilization of different waste forms and its management practices so that student will be able to work effectively with nuclear and environmental engineers in industry or academic institutions.

■ 실습 중심의 교육을 통해 원자력, 플라즈마 및 가속기 공학에서 사용되는 범용 소프트웨어 툴의 기본적인 사용법을 습득한다.
■ 한 학기 내에 다수의 툴에 대한 활용법을 익힘으로써 통합적인 문제해결 능력을 배양한다. 
■ 잘 훈련된 사용자 및 학생들 사이에 툴 사용에 대한 상호 협력의 문화를 배양한다.
Lecture progress plan:
■ Week 1-3: Solidworks을 이용한 Computer-Aided Design (CAD) 실습 및 CFD 프로그램과의 연동 연습 
■ Week 4-6: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) 개념 소개 및 ANSYS CFX 예제를 이용한 CFD 전산모사 실습
■ Week 7: Python 코딩 기초 연습 및 기초 수치해석을 통한 실습
■ Week 8: 중간고사 (과제)
■ Week 9-11: 플라즈마 시뮬레이션, 다중물리 (multiphysics) 전산모사 개념 소개 및 COMSOL 예제를 이용한 실습
■ Week 12-14: 입자가속기 관련 시뮬레이션
■ Week 15: 가속기 설계 툴  
■ Week 16: 기말고사 (과제)

course_operation:
■ 각 툴에 대하여 6회 가량의 튜토리얼 형태의 강의를 진행하며 실습 위주의 과제를 부여함. (주당 2회, 툴당 약 3주)

description: 본 강좌는 대학원생이 학술 연구자로서 연구 문제를 도출하고, 이를 적절한 통계적 방법론을 통해 검증 및 해석할 수 있는 실무적 역량을 배양하는 것을 목표로 한다. 통계학의 수학적 증명보다는 '특정한 연구 문제를 해결하기 위해 어떤 분석 방법을 선택하고 적용해야 하는가'에 초점을 맞춘다. 수강생은 연구 가설 설정, 데이터 수집 및 정제, 분석 결과의 학술적 해석으로 이어지는 사회과학적 관점의 실제 연구 프로세스를 주도적으로 경험함으로써, 자신의 연구 분야에 통계적 방법론을 독립적으로 적용할 수 있는 능력을 갖춘다.

description:
본 과목은 학생들의 원자력 시스템 조건 내에서 핵연료 및 구조재료의 특성 변화에 대한 전반적인 이해를 높이는 것에 목표를 두고 있다. 원자로 재료의 특성을 소개하는 것부터 시작하여, 기초적인 재료의 결정구조 및 결정 결함, 재료 열역학, 재료의 변형과 강화, 재료의 파괴/피로/크립손상, 재료의 조사결함 생성 및 조사손상 메커니즘, 핵연료, 원자로용기 및 내부구조물 조사손상에 대해서 소개할 예정이다. 특히 핵연료의 개발 및 제작, 열적변화와 열전달 성능, 가동 중 부식 현상과 같은 노내 거동과 사용후핵연료의 특성에 대해서 구체적으로 논의할 것이다. 방사선 조사손상을 계산하는 SRIM/TRIM 오픈코드를 직접 활용하는 기회를 학생들에게 제공하여 특정 재료의 조사손상을 시뮬레이션하는 기회를 제공할 것이다. 마지막으로, 국내외의 차세대 원자로로 개발 중인 소형원전, 용윰염 원자로, 고온 헬륨 고속로, 납/납-비스무스 고속로, 소듐 고속로 등에서 논의되고 있는 핵연료 및 구조재료의 개발과 제작 현황 등 실질적인 케이스 스터디를 진행할 예정이다. 
● Providing a comprehensive background for a full-term course on radiation damage and effects in materials.
● Students understand/appreciate the materials science structure/property relationships of key reactor materials, and how these are affected by corrosion and the environment.
● Students learn important factors limiting the lifetime of reactor components, such as radiation damage and corrosion.
● Students understand the specifications and methods of nuclear fuels and structural material fabrication for reliable performance in nuclear power system environments.

Lecture progress plan:
1주 : Introduction & Basic material science
2주 : Diffusion of elements 
3주 : Thermodynamics and phase diagram 
4주 : Elasticity-plasticity theory
5주 : Radiation damage
6주 : Point defect/cross-section
7주 : SRIM simulation
8주 : Fuel fabrciation & Mid-term (close book exam in class)
9주 : Fuel performance and failure
10주 : Fuel chemistry & Fission products
11주 : Heat transfer in nuclear fuel
12주 : Thermal conductivity of fuel & Fission gas release from UO2
13주 : Swelling & Creep behavior
14주 : Zr-alloy cladding & Structural alloys
15주 : Corrosion in nuclear system & Case study presentation
16주 : Final exam (close book exam in class)

description:
1960년에 처음 구현된 레이저(laser –light amplification of stimulated emission of radiation)은 60여년이 지나면서, 과학 기술의 발전에 지대한 공헌을 하였을 뿐만이 아니라 우리 일상뿐만이 아니라 기업의 생산 현장에도 깊숙이 침투해 있다. 
특히 1990년대부터 펨토초 레이저 관련 기술이 본격적으로 개발되고, 새로운 과학 분야 및 기술을 창출함에 따라,  이와 직접 관련하여 4번의 노벨상이 주어졌다 (노벨 물리 학상3번, 노벨 화학상1번) 21세기에 들어서며, 펨토초 레이저를 기반으로 아토초 펄스 발생이 실현됨에 따라, 원자, 분자, 나노구조체에의 전자의 운동을 실시간으로  측정하고자 하는 새로운 과학의 파라다임이 열리고 있고, 원자력, 거대 과학 분야에서도 활발히 사용되어 오고 있다. 
본 강의를 통해서 레이저 광학 및 관련 기술의 기본을 가르치며, 젊은 연구자를 양성하고자 한다.
Lesson Objectives:
1960년에 처음 구현된 레이저(laser –light amplification of stimulated emission of radiation)은 60여년이 지나면서, 과학 기술의 발전에 지대한 공헌을 하였을 뿐만이 아니라 우리 일상뿐만이 아니라 기업의 생산 현장에도 깊숙이 침투해 있다. 
특히 1990년대부터 펨토초 레이저 관련 기술이 본격적으로 개발되고, 새로운 과학 분야 및 기술을 창출함에 따라,  이와 직접 관련하여 4번의 노벨상이 주어졌다 (노벨 물리 학상3번, 노벨 화학상1번) 21세기에 들어서며, 펨토초 레이저를 기반으로 아토초 펄스 발생이 실현됨에 따라, 원자, 분자, 나노구조체에의 전자의 운동을 실시간으로  측정하고자 하는 새로운 과학의 파라다임이 열리고 있고, 원자력, 거대 과학 분야에서도 활발히 사용되어 오고 있다. 
본 강의를 통해서 레이저 광학 및 관련 기술의 기본을 가르치며, 젊은 연구자를 양성하고자 한다.
Lecture progress plan:
1-2주:	introduction to lasers 
3-4주 	Light & Maxwell‘s equations 
5-8주:	Propagation of Light 
9주:	Geometrical Optics / Gaussian Optics
10주: 	Interference & Superposition
11주:    diffraction          			
12-16주:    ultrafast optics
		mode locking, dispersion, autocorrelation, 
     		ultrafast pulse measurement, 
		attosecond pusle generation and applications, etc.
grading: 출석, quiz
references: 담당 교수가 만든 강의 및 실습 교재 사용

description:

- The lecture aims to provide basic knowledge and understanding of safety assessment so as to be   built basic capability as a safety expert for nuclear regulation.

description: 포스텍 학생들이 모두 우수한 인재이고 공학 지식에 기반하여 미래 리더로서 성장할 것은 분명합니다. 다만, 한국 입시 교육 시스템에서 우리는 실제 자신의 모습을 가만히 들여다 보기도 아려웠고 자신의 잠재성을 탐구해볼 수 없었던 것도 사실입니다. 이에 확연하게 바뀐 세계적 흐름안에서 미래를 디자인 해야하는 학생들이 스스로 자신의 욕망과 성격, 그리고 투지에 대한 물음을 던지고 그것에 대답하는 과정을 가지면서 자기자신의 성장에 대한 탐지 경험을 가질 수 있는 시간을 가지려 합니다.

description:
1. Understand human-centered design principles and explain how human needs, cognitive characteristics, behaviors, and contexts inform the design of interactive systems.

2. Investigate users and real-world contexts using appropriate qualitative and user-research methods, including interviews, observation, thinking-aloud protocols, stakeholder analysis, and personas.

3. Translate user insights into design requirements by identifying problems, stakeholders, interactions, user journeys, scenarios, and functional requirements.

4. Apply an iterative design process to move from problem discovery and definition to concept development, prototyping, evaluation, and refinement.

5. Design and evaluate interactive experiences by considering usefulness, usability, affect, and broader dimensions of user experience.

6. Explore emerging forms of human–AI interaction involving LLMs, AI agents, MCP, and Physical AI, and critically consider how these technologies can be incorporated into human-centered solutions.

7. Develop and communicate a working prototype that demonstrates a coherent connection among user research, design requirements, technological possibilities, and design decisions.

description:
This course provides innovative analysis of devices and circuits in electronic engineering, which is fundamental for IT engineering students. This course covers the fundamental physics of devices with materials and interpretation methods of electronic circuits. 
* Note: This semester, it is only available to undergraduate students in the Department of IT Convergence. Other students can take the class starting next semester.

이 교과목에서는 IT공학도로서 기본적으로 알고 있어야 하는 전자공학의 소자 및 회로의 전반적인 내용에 대해서 다룬다. 전자회로의 기초 개념과 해석 방법, 트랜지스터, 연산증폭기와 같은 중요 소자의 동작원리 및 디지털 논리회로를 다루고 전자소자 재료의 제반 특성, 빛과 물질의 상호작용, 반도체, 도체, 비등방성 물질, 비선형광학 물질의 구조와 특성에 대해 기초소자(Resistor, Capacitor, Inductor, PN diode, BJT, MOSFET 등)를 바탕으로 기초이론과 개념을 가르치는 것을 목적으로 한다.

이 교과목에서는 IT공학도로서 기본적으로 알고 있어야 하는 전자공학의 소자 및 회로의 전반적인 내용에 대해서 다룬다. 전자회로의 기초 개념과 해석 방법, 트랜지스터, 연산증폭기와 같은 중요 소자의 동작원리 및 디지털 논리회로를 다루고 전자소자 재료의 제반 특성, 빛과 물질의 상호작용, 반도체, 도체, 비등방성 물질, 비선형광학 물질의 구조와 특성에 대해 기초소자(Resistor, Capacitor, Inductor, PN diode, BJT, MOSFET 등)를 바탕으로 기초이론과 개념을 가르치는 것을 목적으로 한다.
Lecture progress plan:
- 1주:  Introduction: what is electronics? / applications of electronics and electronic components       
 - 2~3주 : Semiconductor Device Physics
- 4주 : Diodes with circuit analysis techniques
- 5주 : Capacitor and inductor with analyzing transient circuit
- 6주 : Transistor biasing and transistor amplifier circuits 
- 7주 : Midterm Exam
- 8~9주 : Field Effect Transistors 
- 9주~10주 : Integrated circuit design with the BJT
- 11주~12주: Integrated circuit design with the MOSFET
- 13~14주 : The differential stage and OP amplifier  
- 15주 : Basic Logic circuits (CMOS inverter, CMOS logic gates)
- 16주 :Final Exam

Midterm exam (40%), final exam (50%), attendance (10%)

중간고사 (40%), 기말고사 (50%), 출석 (10%)

description:
이 과목은 인공지능 관련 연구 과목입니다. 본인이 하고 싶은 인공지능 관련 연구를 하면서 수업 학점을 받을 수 있는 좋은 기회입니다. 강의 내용은 인공지능 방법 중 실질적인 Neural Network 기반 방법 (CNN, RNN 등) 에 사용되는 원리 이론, 연산 방법/이유, 연산량 및 이러한 연산을 잘 지원할 수 있는 컴퓨터 프로그래밍 방법 및 컴퓨터 구조에 대한 내용으로 구성되어 있습니다. 각 학생은 본인의 연구 주제를 정하고 세 번 (Proposal, Progress, Final) 발표하는 기회가 있을 것입니다. 강의 언어는 영어이지만 한글 요약 및 추가 설명도 있을 것입니다.
(This is a research class where the student can pursue any research work related to Artificial Intelligence while getting course credit. Lectures will focus on practical AI Neural Network methods, their theoretical foundations, the computations involved and the reason for the use of such computations, amount of computational operations used, their programming methods, and the computer architectures necessary to support such computations. The student will have opportunities to present his/her research work 3 times during the class (Proposal, Progress, Final). The course language is English with Korean summaries.)

- PBL기반 수업으로 기업-멘토 프로젝트 멘토링이 격주간으로 수행됨.
- 이 격주 사이에 학생들이 자신이 수행하고 있는 프로젝트에 대해 함께 내용을 공유하고 아이디어를 나누며 솔루션을 만들어가는 집단지성 수업임.
- 새로운 지식과 정보, 솔루션에 대한 문제 해결 역량을 배움.
- 10주차 크로스터치 워크샵, 16차 오픈클래스를 통해 학기 동안 수행한 결과를 기업멘토, 참여교수, 솔루션 스튜디오 수강생 등 모두 모여 발표하고 공유하며 상호 점검 및 피드백 진행 예정임.
- 이 과목은 국내외 선도적인 기업 및 연구기관과의 협력을 기반으로 운영됨. 주요 참여기업으로는 쓰리브룩스테라퓨틱스, 바이오브릭스, 일리미스테라퓨틱스, 지멘스헬시니어스, 에스포항병원, 헬시버디 등 총 6개 기관이 있으며, 각 기업은 프로젝트 주제와 관련된 전문 지식과 실질적인 문제해결 경험을 제공할 예정임.

description:
기존 대학원 공대 수업과는 다른 Project Based Learning 수업입니다. 중간고사나 기말고사가 없는 대신, 매주 수업에서 다양한 문제를 접하고 교수-학생이 함께 아이디어를 모색하고 집단지성으로 문제를 해결하는 과정을 몸으로 체험하는 수업이라고 생각하시면 좋을 것 같습니다. 
공학지식인들의 역활은 이제 단순히 직장 소속의 엔지니어를 넘어 새로운 리더의 역활을 요구하고 있다고 여겨집니다. 세계사적 흐름이기도 하고 우리에게도 꼭 필요한 자세이자 태도인것 같습니다. 이에 곧 사회로 진출하여 새로운 지성인의 자리에서 미래 리더의 역활을 수행할 학생들이라는 전제하에, 공학 지식의 틀을 넘어 전체를 아우르는 지식 융합적 태도와 유연한 지성을 훈련하는 시간을 가지려 합니다.

공학지식인들의 역활은 이제 단순히 직장 소속의 엔지니어를 넘어 새로운 리더의 역활을 요구하고 있다고 여겨집니다. 세계사적 흐름이기도 하고 우리에게도 꼭 필요한 자세이자 태도인것 같습니다. 이에 곧 사회로 진출하여 새로운 지성인의 자리에서 미래 리더의 역활을 수행할 학생들이라는 전제하에, 공학 지식의 틀을 넘어 전체를 아우르는 지식 융합적 태도와 유연한 지성을 훈련하는 시간을 가지려 합니다.

description:
Class Objective: 

According to UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, 
“The practice of physical education and sport is a fundamental right for all.”
“Adequate facilities and equipment are essential to physical education and sport.”
(International Charter of Physical Education and Sport, Paris, 21 Nov. 1978)

As above, sport is a key element to lead a healthy and happy life for us; it is our basic rights. 
Sport makes our lives healthy, and in turn, mentally wealthy. Then, “how” can we promote sports activities in our lives? This class is trying to find the answer in the convergence engineering of sports and ICT. 

	Sports = all forms of usually competitive physical activity 
	Engineering = Technical application of math and physics to solve problems
	Sports engineering is concerned with the research and development of technologies for the sports industry.

“Engineering skill first and knowledge of sport thereafter.”

Class Objectives:
1)	To understand a paradigm shifting in sports industry: providing the integrated knowledge of state-of-the-art science & technology into sports required to open up new frontiers of sports industry.
2)	To perform pioneering research to solve difficult unmet needs for sports industry: multidisciplinary research with imagination in the fields of sports and engineering knowledge that can provide solutions possible to be applied in creative and ingenious ways.
3)	To cultivate talented individuals who lead the future IT industry: develop and demonstrate the creative solutions via teamwork.

description: This course provides an in-depth understanding of the design and implementation of modern operating systems (OS), with a focus on the Linux kernel and related system software. It covers key technical topics essential for developing efficient kernel and system-level software, including kernel data structures, system call interfaces, device drivers, memory management, CPU scheduling, file systems, and synchronization mechanisms. The course also introduces practical skills for Linux kernel programming, such as building kernel modules, implementing character and block device drivers, and managing kernel memory and concurrency.

description:
"Questions in discrete geometry typically involve finite sets of points, lines, circles, planes, or other simple geometric o
bjects. For example, one can ask, what is the largest number of regions into which n lines can partition the plane, or what
is the minimum possible number of distinct distances occurring among n points in the plane (the former question is easy, t
he latter one is hard). More complicated objects are investigated too, such as convex polytopes or finite families of convex
sets. The emphasis is on "combinatorial" properties: which of the given objects intersect, or how many points are needed t
o intersect all of them, and so on. Characteristics like angle, distance, curvature, or volume, ubiquitous in other areas o
f geometry, are usually not of primary interest, although they can serve as useful tools.
Many questions in discrete geometry are very natural and worth studying for their own sake. Some of them, such as the struct
ure of 3-dimensional convex polytopes, go back to the Antiquity, and a lot of them are motivated by other areas of mathemat
ics. To a working mathematician or computer scientist, the contemporary discrete geometry offers results and techniques of
great diversity, a useful enhancement of the "bag of tricks" for attacking problems in her or his field."
- from the preface of "Lectures on Discrete Geometry"

Computational geometry is the study of design and analysis of algorithms dealing with geometric objects.
It emerged as a sub-discipline of theoretical computer science from 1970s, and has grown into a recognized
research discipline in computer sciecen and applied mathematics, with a large community of active researchers.
It had developed in several directions and forged links with other application domains such as computer aided design,
robotics, computer graphics, virtual reality, computer vision, bio-informatics, and geographic information system.
We believe that knowledge of computational geometry is important to solve geometric problems in application areas
efficiently. This course, therefore, covers a number of core geometric techniques that have been used to solve problems
from application areas, frome which we expect that, given a geometric problem, students are able to understand the
geometric properties of it and apply a proper algorithmic techniques and data structures.
We start with an introduction to computational geometry and study plane sweep algorithms. Then we cover the fundamental
techniques presented in the following chapters of the textbook.

Algorithm design and analysis
